records.place: Schwaigern, on the Heuchelberg west of Heilbronn, Württemberg

wine.name: Schwaigerner Ruthe Lemberger GG
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Ruthe, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Schwaigern
wine.grapes: Lemberger alone, the grape Austria calls Blaufränkisch.
wine.sites: The Ruthe, about a kilometre from the family's castle on the south facing Heuchelberg at Schwaigern: partly terraced, at 20 to 40 per cent and some 250 to 310 metres, on Gipskeuper with coloured marl above, sheltered from north and west winds. The house holds it whole.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented on the skins in the traditional way. By the sheets of several vintages the wine is then raised in barriques, new and used, for well over a year, in the vaulted cellars beneath the family's palace at Schwaigern, before it is bottled dry.
wine.glass: Wild cherry, cassis and blackberry with black pepper and a smoky note from the barrel; dense and juicy, with fine, firm tannin and taut acidity, the fruit held in by the grape's natural freshness.
wine.ageing: Tight and oaky in its first years, it opens after five years or so and keeps for a decade and more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The single vineyard on the Heuchelberg at Schwaigern, first named in a record of 1385.

records.table: Graf Neipperg's Ruthe Lemberger GG comes from a steep slope of the Heuchelberg near the family castle, Lemberger being Württemberg's name for Blaufränkisch. Raised in barriques, it shows wild cherry, cassis and pepper with firm, fresh tannin; decant a young bottle.
records.story: The counts of Neipperg take their name from a castle on the Heuchelberg above Schwaigern, built, as the family tells it, in the thirteenth century with vineyards around it. In 1702 the family built its palace at Schwaigern over the moats of a medieval castle, and its vaulted cellars have held the family's barrels for generations. In 1726 the Emperor Charles VI raised Wilhelm Reinhard von Neipperg (1684 to 1774), a general in Vienna, to the rank of count. By the family's own account it was in that century that it brought Lemberger to Württemberg; it is told as the house's tradition, not a record. In 1806 the county passed to the Kingdom of Württemberg, and in 1821 the count's grandson, Adam Albert von Neipperg (1775 to 1829), an Austrian general, married Marie Louise, the widow of Napoleon. In 1971 a later count bought Château Canon-La-Gaffelière and other estates at Saint-Émilion, and a branch of the family has made wine in Bordeaux ever since. At Schwaigern the Ruthe, first named in 1385, is the house's own vineyard, and its Lemberger Grosses Gewächs is the wine through which the family speaks for the grape it claims to have brought.

Lemberger is Blaufränkisch under its Württemberg name; Schwarzriesling, the region's other red with a misleading name, is Pinot Meunier.
That the family brought Lemberger to Württemberg is the house's tradition, not a documented fact.

wine.name: Untertürkheimer Gips Marienglas Riesling GG
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from Gips Marienglas, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Untertürkheim
wine.sites: Gips Marienglas at Untertürkheim on the edge of Stuttgart, facing south to south west on Gipskeuper, the pale gypsum marl of the Keuper, where gypsum was once quarried; the house holds the site alone.
wine.making: By the house's sheets the wine is fermented with wild yeasts in large wooden casks and raised in them on its lees for about ten months before it is bottled dry. Under the VDP's rule a Grosses Gewächs is never released before September of the year after the harvest.
wine.glass: Yellow apple, white peach and lime peel over a chalky, salty note from the gypsum; dry and firm, with ripe acidity and a long, slightly phenolic finish.
wine.ageing: Closed in its first two or three years, it opens with time and keeps for ten years and more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a large white wine glass.

records.table: Aldinger of Fellbach makes its Gips Marienglas Riesling GG at Untertürkheim on the edge of Stuttgart, on pale gypsum marl; Marienglas is the old German name for clear gypsum crystal. Dry, firm and chalky, it shows Württemberg's white side.
records.story: By the family's own account an ancestor, Bentz der Aldinger, was already tending vines at Fellbach in 1492, the year Columbus reached America, and the house calls itself the oldest estate in Fellbach. Fellbach lies against the north eastern edge of Stuttgart, and the family's vineyards run across the Lämmler above the town and over the boundary to Untertürkheim on the Neckar. There, by its own account, the family bought the Gips in 1973, a site it calls the oldest documented vineyard of Stuttgart, on the pale gypsum marl of the Keuper, named for the gypsum once quarried there. Gips is the German word for gypsum, and Marienglas is the old name for its clear crystal, once set as glass before pictures of the Virgin. In 2002 the VDP, an association of German wine estates, defined the Grosses Gewächs as a dry wine from its classified vineyards, and from the 2012 vintage it ranked its sites on a ladder modelled on Burgundy, with Grosse Lage as its highest step. Gips Marienglas is one of those, and its Riesling stands beside the house's Lemberger from the Lämmler. In a region that plants more red grapes than white, it shows a sommelier that Württemberg's Keuper can carry a dry Riesling of weight.

The VDP's page and wein.plus give Bentz der Aldinger and 1492; the house's own Sekt page says the same. That Gips is the oldest documented vineyard of Stuttgart is the house's claim on its VDP page, told as such.

wine.name: Fellbacher Lämmler Spätburgunder GG
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Lämmler, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Fellbach
wine.grapes: Spätburgunder alone, the German name for Pinot Noir.
wine.sites: Old vines in the Brenner, a parcel within the Lämmler above Fellbach, whose slopes face south to west and run from heavy Gipskeuper up through reed sandstone to Stubensandstein, with coloured marl.
wine.making: Fermented on the skins with wild yeasts, partly as whole bunches, then raised for about eighteen months in 300 litre casks, by the house's recent sheets half new and half used, and bottled unfiltered.
wine.glass: Red cherry, raspberry and wild strawberry over forest floor, rose petal and a smoky note; silky and fresh, with fine tannin and a long, gently savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Open enough to enjoy after four or five years, it gains depth over a decade and keeps longer in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a Burgundy glass.

records.table: Schnaitmann's Lämmler Spätburgunder GG is Pinot Noir from old vines in the Brenner parcel above Fellbach, on Keuper marl and sandstone. Fermented partly as whole bunches and raised in 300 litre casks, it is silky, fresh and cherry scented.
records.story: The Schnaitmanns are an old Fellbach family: by the house's account the register of the town's church records a Hans Schnaitmann born in 1550. For generations the family grew grapes and, like most of Fellbach's growers, brought them to the town's co-operative, founded in 1858. The estate under the family's own label is young. In 1997 the founder, an heir of that long line of growers, began to make and bottle his own wine from a small holding, and bottles with the Schnaitmann label went out from 1998. By the house's account it began organic farming in 2008. The house built its name on reds from the Keuper of the Kappelberg, Spätburgunder and Lemberger above all, at a time when Württemberg was known mostly for light Trollinger poured by the quarter litre. When the VDP ranked its vineyards from the 2012 vintage, the Lämmler became Fellbach's Grosse Lage. The Spätburgunder from its old vines in the Brenner is the wine that shows a sommelier what Pinot Noir from Württemberg's Keuper can be.

wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Michaelsberg, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Cleebronn
wine.grapes: Lemberger alone, the grape Austria calls Blaufränkisch.
wine.sites: The Michaelsberg at Cleebronn, a lone hill crowned by a Romanesque church and known locally as the guardian of the Zabergäu: a steep south facing slope of 40 to 50 per cent at 335 to 385 metres, on coloured marl, a limy, stony Keuper clay laid over the Gipskeuper.
wine.making: The house has raised its leading reds in small oak since 1985. By one recent critic's sheet the Michaelsberg Lemberger spends about a year in tonneaux, then some ten months in a large wooden cask, and rests in bottle for over a year before release.
wine.glass: Blackberry, sour cherry and plum with black pepper, violet and a graphite note; dense and juicy, with firm, fine tannin, lively acidity and a stony, slightly salty finish.
wine.ageing: Released only after a long rest, it is approachable young but gains over eight to ten years and more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Dautel of Bönnigheim makes its Michaelsberg Lemberger GG on the lone hill at Cleebronn crowned by a Romanesque church, on coloured Keuper marl. Raised in tonneaux and a large cask, it is dense, peppery and fresh; decant it young.
records.story: By the house's own account the Dautels have grown vines at Bönnigheim, between the Stromberg and the Heuchelberg, since 1510, and the estate counts its generations from that year. For most of the twentieth century the family's grapes went to the local co-operative, as most of Württemberg's did. In the 1970s an heir of the family left the co-operative and began to make and bottle the family's wine himself. In 1985, by the house's account, he began to raise his leading reds in barriques, early for the region, and in 1999 the estate was admitted to the VDP. In 2010 his son came home from his studies at Geisenheim to work beside him and later took the estate on, and the first Grosses Gewächs from the Michaelsberg at Cleebronn followed with the 2010 vintage. The hill, a landmark of the Zabergäu valley with its church at the peak, gives a Lemberger the house calls its signature red, early bottlings of which carried the name St. Michaelsfeder. It is a Lemberger to show a sommelier how Württemberg's serious red behaves on Keuper marl: dense, peppery and fresh rather than heavy.

records.place: Stetten, Kernen im Remstal, east of Stuttgart, Württemberg

wine.name: Stettener Pulvermächer Riesling GG
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Pulvermächer, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Stetten
wine.sites: The Pulvermächer at Stetten, a terraced slope facing south to south west in a side valley of the Rems below the ruin of the Yburg, at about 330 to 370 metres, on lean sandstone and coloured marl of the Keuper.
wine.making: Picked by hand, pressed as whole bunches and fermented with wild yeasts in the house's traditional large old wooden casks, then raised in them on its lees for about a year before it is bottled dry.
wine.glass: Lime, green apple and white peach over wet stone and a smoky, slightly flinty note; lean and taut, with bright acidity and a long, salty finish.
wine.ageing: Tight in its first years, it opens after three to five and keeps for a decade and more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The vineyard at Stetten, its name an old word for a blaster in the neighbouring quarry.
The village of Kernen in the Rems valley where the house and the vineyard lie.
Often shortened to GG: a dry wine of the VDP from a vineyard it ranks Grosse Lage.

records.table: Karl Haidle's Pulvermächer Riesling GG grows on old terraces below the Yburg ruin at Stetten in the Rems valley, on lean Keuper sandstone. Fermented with wild yeasts in large old casks, it is lean, smoky and salty; serve it cool.
records.story: The estate takes the name of its founder, Karl Haidle, who in 1949 began with a small plot of vines at Stetten in the Rems valley and, as the house tells it, set out to sell his own wine in bottle. As the house tells it he died young, and in 1968 his son took the estate over and with his wife built it up across the slopes around Stetten. The Pulvermächer, first recorded in 1650, lies beside the village under the ruin of the Yburg, and by the VDP's account its name is an old word for a blaster, tied to the neighbouring quarry where rock was blasted. Its old stone terraces hold the day's warmth, and its lean sandstone gives Riesling of more tension than weight. When the VDP ranked its vineyards from the 2012 vintage the Pulvermächer became a Grosse Lage. In 2014 the founder's grandson took over and turned the estate to organic farming, and by the house's account it has been farmed biodynamically since 2020. In a region known for red wine, the Pulvermächer is the Riesling a sommelier should know from the Rems valley.

traps: The Pulvermächer is a Riesling site at Stetten in the Rems valley, not at Fellbach or on the Neckar at Stuttgart.
Pulvermächer is an old word for a blaster who worked with powder in a neighbouring quarry; it has nothing to do with the dust of the soil.
Weingut Karl Haidle bears the founder's name; the estate has passed to his son and his grandson since.

questions.q: A guest asks how Karl Haidle ferments its Pulvermächer Riesling GG. Which answer fits the house's sheets?
opts: With wild yeasts in large old wooden casks
With cultured yeasts in new barriques
In concrete eggs with skin contact
In stainless steel, then sweetened back
questions.exp: The house presses whole bunches and ferments with wild yeasts in its traditional large old casks, raising the wine on its lees for about a year; a Grosses Gewächs is always dry, never sweetened back.

questions.q: By the VDP's account, what lies behind the name of the Pulvermächer at Stetten?
opts: Blasting with powder in a neighbouring quarry
A powder mill of the dukes of Württemberg
The fine dust of its sandstone soil
A founder of the estate named Pulver
questions.exp: The VDP ties the name to the neighbouring quarry, where rock was blasted; it does not come from the soil's dust or from a person.

report: Read through search summaries of the house's estate page, its 75th anniversary page, its Pulvermächer sheets of 2017 and 2019, an Eichelmann article on its site, the VDP's Pulvermächer and estate pages, wein.plus and the Stuttgarter Zeitung; 4 of the author's 35 searches went to this house.

1949 rests on the house, Eichelmann and the Stuttgarter Zeitung's 75 years; wein.plus gives 1953 with a nursery as its first business, noted for the checker. The start of about half a hectare is the house's and Eichelmann's; wein.plus gives one hectare.

Karl Haidle's dates were not found in two sources, so the story gives none; he is named because the house bears his name, and his early death rests on the house's page. The son's takeover in 1968 rests on Eichelmann alone and is hedged as one account.

The slope: the house gives up to 60 per cent and 330 to 360 metres, the VDP up to 25 per cent and 350 to 370 metres, so the record says terraced and about 330 to 370 metres. First recorded in 1650 is the VDP's; another account gives 1420.
That the founder was the first in the valley to bottle his own wine is the house's claim, told as such; the claim that he first planted Kerner there is left out.
A merchant's listing calls the Schilfsandstein the former Pulvermächer; the house's own sheet places it east of Stetten on reed sandstone, which the record follows.
Living people met: Hans Haidle, Susanne Haidle, Wolfgang Haidle and Moritz Haidle, for people.json; none is named in prose.

The VDP's German page says the old Gewann was enlarged in the 1971 consolidation into a single vineyard of 37 hectares; the Grosse Lage is the classified core. Not added.
